title: BIST over a chip's life
summary: BIST is not only a factory tool. The same hardware tests the chip during **burn-in**, at the **customer**, at every **power-on** and even **while the system runs** — which is why cars, planes and data centres depend on it. But BIST also has a **price**.
objectives: Explain the bathtub curve and why burn-in is done.
Describe power-on and periodic self-test and why safety standards such as ISO 26262 need them.
List the costs of BIST and weigh them against its benefits.

blocks.md: Some chips pass every test in the factory and still fail after a few weeks. They carry **weak spots** — a thin wire, a marginal oxide — that work today but break soon. Reliability engineers draw this with the **bathtub curve**:

steps.title: Early failures
steps.md: At the start of life the failure rate is high: the **weak** chips fail first. This is called *infant mortality*.

steps.title: Useful life
steps.md: Once the weak chips are gone, the failure rate is low and nearly constant — random failures only.

steps.title: Wear-out
steps.md: After many years the transistors and wires **age** (hot carriers, electromigration, oxide wear) and failures rise again.

steps.title: Burn-in
steps.md: **Burn-in** runs the chips for hours at high temperature and voltage in the factory. This *ages* them quickly, so the weak ones fail **before shipping** — not at the customer.

blocks.md:
During burn-in the chips should be **active**, so that the stress reaches every transistor. But a burn-in oven holds hundreds of chips on large boards, and a full tester channel for every pin of every chip is impossible.

With BIST it is easy: each chip needs only power, a clock and a *start* signal, and it **exercises itself**. The board just collects *pass/fail* from each socket.

blocks.title: BIST makes burn-in useful
blocks.md: Running MBIST and LBIST in the oven both **stresses** the logic and memories and **detects** the chips that broke during the stress.

steps.title: 1. Wafer sort and final test
steps.md: In the factory the tester starts MBIST and LBIST through a few pins and reads the results — the work you saw in Topic 2.

steps.title: 2. Burn-in
steps.md: In the oven the chips run their own BIST again and again while they are stressed.

steps.title: 3. Board and system test
steps.md: The customer solders the chip on a board. The **same** BIST can be started through the JTAG port — no expensive tester needed.

steps.title: 4. Power-on self-test (POST)
steps.md: Every time the system is switched on, the chip tests itself **before** it starts its real job. A car's brake controller does this at every key-on.

steps.title: 5. Periodic test while running
steps.md: Some systems cannot wait for the next start-up. They run **short** tests in idle moments, one block at a time, saving and restoring the block's state around the test.

steps.title: 6. Shut-down test and diagnosis
steps.md: When the system turns off there is time for longer tests. Results are stored, so a service engineer can later see what failed.

blocks.md: Why test a chip that already passed in the factory? Because chips **age**, are hit by radiation, heat and voltage spikes. In most products a rare failure is annoying. In a car, a plane or a medical device it can **hurt people**.

The functional-safety standard **ISO 26262** asks how well the chip detects its own faults. Each safety function gets an **ASIL** level, from A (lowest) to D (highest, e.g. braking, steering). The higher the level, the more faults the safety mechanisms must catch:
**Latent** faults are faults that hide — for example in a safety mechanism that is not used until something else breaks. Power-on and periodic **LBIST and MBIST** are a main way to find them.

tabs.label: Data centres
tabs.md: Servers run for years without a break. Memory BIST at boot finds weak cells and **repairs** them with spare rows (MBIST course), and periodic tests catch **silent data corruption** — a core that computes wrong results without crashing.

tabs.label: Aerospace and medical
tabs.md: Space electronics is hit by radiation; medical devices must prove they work before every use. Both rely on **self-test at start-up** and during operation, together with error-correcting memories.

blocks.md: BIST hardware is not free. Before adding it, designers weigh what it **costs** against what it **gives**:

items.title: Area
items.md: Pattern generators, comparators, controllers and multiplexers take silicon. MBIST for many small memories and LBIST with test points typically add a **few percent** of chip area. Sharing one controller between several memories reduces it.

items.title: Test power
items.md: During BIST far more flip-flops toggle than in normal use. The current can be **higher than in functional mode**, causing voltage drop and false failures. BIST must be designed to limit power — test fewer blocks at once, or slow down.

items.title: Timing
items.md: Test multiplexers sit in front of memories and flip-flops. Each adds a little **delay** to the functional path, which can reduce the maximum clock frequency if not handled carefully.

items.title: Design and verification effort
items.md: BIST must be inserted, connected, verified and documented for every block. Commercial EDA tools automate most of it (Tessent, TestMAX, Modus), but the work remains.

items.title: Test quality limits
items.md: Pseudo-random LBIST patterns miss some hard-to-test faults; it may need **test points** or extra deterministic patterns from the tester (LBIST course).

blocks.title: The usual answer
blocks.md: For memories, MBIST is used in **almost every** modern chip — there is no other practical way to test them. LBIST is used where in-field test is required (automotive, aerospace, servers) or where test time is very expensive.

questions.text: What is the purpose of burn-in?
options: Make weak chips fail in the factory instead of at the customer.
Measure the yield of the wafer.
questions.explain: Burn-in ages the chips quickly so that the **early failures** of the bathtub curve happen before shipping.

questions.text: Why is BIST especially useful during burn-in?
options: Each chip needs only power, a clock and a start signal, so hundreds can run at once in the oven.
BIST works only at high temperature.
Burn-in ovens contain a full tester for every pin.

questions.text: A car's brake controller tests itself every time the driver starts the car. This is called …
Under ISO 26262, a safety function with ASIL D must detect a larger share of faults than one with ASIL B.
questions.explain: ASIL D is the highest level: e.g. ≥ 99 % single-point fault metric versus ≥ 90 % for ASIL B.

questions.text: Why does a periodic test during operation test only **one block at a time**, for a short time?
options: The system must keep doing its job; the tested block is unavailable during the test.
BIST can only test one block in its whole life.
Short tests detect more faults than long ones.
The tester can only connect to one block.
